findings.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution inputs
findings.attack_path: Authenticated user POSTs to /contributions with preTax/afterTax/roth values that are passed directly to eval() in handleContributionsUpdate. Supplying a payload such as 'global.process.mainModule.require("child_process").execSync("id")' executes arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process, giving the attacker code execution and a pivot to the host and database.
findings.remediation: Replace eval() with parseInt()/Number() parsing of the numeric fields (the commented fix in contributions.js). Never pass request input to eval, Function, or vm. Validate and bound the parsed integers before use.

findings.title: NoSQL injection via $where in allocations threshold
findings.attack_path: GET /allocations/:userId?threshold=... builds a MongoDB $where clause by string-concatenating the unsanitized threshold into a JavaScript expression (this.stocks > '${threshold}'). An attacker injects '1'; return true' to dump all allocations, or '0';while(true){}'' to run an infinite loop server-side, causing data disclosure or denial of service.
findings.remediation: Remove the $where server-side JavaScript query. Parse threshold with parseInt and bound it (0-99), then use a structured query operator ($gt) instead of string interpolation, as shown in the commented fix in allocations-dao.js.

findings.title: Cleartext password storage and plaintext credential comparison
findings.attack_path: addUser stores the raw password field in the users collection and validateLogin compares fromDB === fromUser in cleartext. Any read access to MongoDB (injection, backup theft, insider, exposed instance) yields every user's plaintext password, enabling account takeover and credential reuse across systems. bcrypt-nodejs is a dependency but the hashing code is commented out.
findings.remediation: Hash passwords with bcrypt (bcrypt.hashSync with a generated salt) on signup and use bcrypt.compareSync on login, per the commented fix in user-dao.js. Migrate existing records on next login.

findings.title: Stored cross-site scripting via globally disabled template autoescaping
findings.attack_path: swig.setDefaults({autoescape:false}) in server.js disables output encoding for all {{ }} expressions. A user saves a script payload in profile firstName/lastName (rendered in profile.html, dashboard, benefits, allocations) or a memo (rendered via marked(doc.memo) in memos.html). When another user or admin views the page the script executes in their session, allowing session-cookie theft and admin account compromise.
findings.remediation: Re-enable swig autoescape (autoescape:true) and only mark specific trusted fields safe. Contextually encode user data for HTML/URL/JS sinks. Keep marked sanitize enabled with a current, non-vulnerable Markdown library.

findings.title: Insecure direct object reference on /allocations/:userId
findings.attack_path: displayAllocations reads userId from the URL path parameter rather than the session, then returns that user's allocations (joined with userName/firstName/lastName from the users collection). Any logged-in user iterates the numeric userId to read every other user's financial allocations and identity data.
findings.remediation: Derive userId from req.session.userId, not req.params, per the commented fix in allocations.js. Add an authorization check that the requested resource belongs to the authenticated principal.

findings.title: Missing function-level access control on /benefits admin page
findings.attack_path: GET/POST /benefits are protected only by isLoggedIn; the isAdmin middleware exists but is not applied (the admin-guarded route is commented out in index.js). Any authenticated non-admin user views all employees and updates arbitrary users' benefitStartDate via POST /benefits, a privileged HR function.
findings.remediation: Add the isAdmin middleware to both /benefits routes (the commented fix in index.js). Enforce role checks server-side on every privileged function, not just by hiding UI links.

findings.title: Server-side request forgery in research stock-symbol fetch
findings.attack_path: displayResearch concatenates req.query.url + req.query.symbol and passes it directly to needle.get, then writes the response body back to the client. An attacker sets url to an internal address (e.g. http://localhost or a cloud metadata endpoint) to reach internal services, scan the network, or exfiltrate metadata/credentials through the proxied response.
findings.remediation: Do not accept the target URL from the client. Use a fixed allowlisted upstream base URL and append only a validated symbol token. Block requests to private/link-local ranges and disable redirects.

findings.title: Sensitive PII (SSN, DOB, bank account/routing) stored unencrypted at rest
findings.attack_path: profile-dao.updateUser writes ssn, dob, bankAcc, and bankRouting to the users collection in cleartext (the crypto/encrypt helpers are commented out). Database read access (via injection TM-002, backup exposure, or insider) discloses regulated personal and financial data for every user.
findings.remediation: Encrypt SSN/DOB/bank fields at rest using authenticated encryption with a managed key (per the commented crypto helpers, but with a per-record IV and a KMS-held key rather than a hard-coded cryptoKey). Apply field-level access controls and minimize retention.

findings.title: Application served over plaintext HTTP with no TLS
findings.attack_path: server.js creates an http.createServer only; the https configuration is commented out. Credentials, session cookies, SSN, and bank data traverse the network in cleartext. A network-position attacker (shared Wi-Fi, on-path proxy) captures credentials and session tokens and hijacks accounts.
findings.remediation: Terminate TLS (https.createServer with the artifacts/cert key/cert, or a TLS-terminating reverse proxy/load balancer), redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and set HSTS via helmet.

findings.title: Missing HTTP security headers (clickjacking, MIME sniffing, no CSP)
findings.attack_path: All helmet middleware (frameguard, noCache, contentSecurityPolicy, hsts, nosniff) and x-powered-by removal are commented out in server.js. The app can be framed for clickjacking, has no CSP to blunt the stored XSS in TM-004, and leaks the Express fingerprint, easing targeted attacks.
findings.remediation: Enable helmet with frameguard, a restrictive contentSecurityPolicy, noSniff, and hsts, and call app.disable('x-powered-by').

findings.title: Insecure session management: weak cookie flags and no session regeneration on login
findings.attack_path: The express-session config omits cookie.httpOnly and cookie.secure (so the cookie is readable by JS via the TM-004 XSS and sent over cleartext HTTP), uses saveUninitialized:true, and handleLoginRequest sets req.session.userId without calling req.session.regenerate(). An attacker who fixes or steals a pre-auth session id retains it post-login (session fixation) and can ride the cookie after XSS theft.
findings.remediation: Set cookie.httpOnly and cookie.secure, add a sane maxAge, set saveUninitialized:false, use a non-default cookie name, and call req.session.regenerate() on successful login (the commented fix in session.js).

findings.title: Hard-coded application secrets in source (session and crypto keys)
findings.attack_path: config/env/all.js hard-codes cookieSecret ('session_cookie_secret_key_here') and cryptoKey ('a_secure_key_for_crypto_here') in the repository. Anyone with source access can forge or tamper with signed session cookies and decrypt any data encrypted with the static key, defeating session integrity and any at-rest encryption.
findings.remediation: Move cookieSecret and cryptoKey to environment variables or a secrets manager, generate high-entropy values per environment, and rotate the committed values that are now public.

findings.title: Regular expression denial of service in profile bank-routing validation
findings.attack_path: handleProfileUpdate validates bankRouting with /([0-9]+)+\#/, a nested quantifier vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. POSTing a long run of digits with no trailing '#' (e.g. '11111111111111111111111111') pins the single-threaded Node event loop at 100% CPU, blocking all other requests.
findings.remediation: Replace the regex with a linear pattern such as /([0-9]+)\#/ (the commented fix in profile.js) and bound input length before testing.

findings.title: Open redirect on /learn endpoint
findings.attack_path: GET /learn does res.redirect(req.query.url) with no validation. An attacker crafts a NodeGoat /learn link whose url points to a phishing or malware site; victims trust the legitimate origin and follow the redirect, enabling credential-phishing and OAuth-token theft.
findings.remediation: Redirect only to an allowlist of internal paths/hosts, or map a fixed set of named resources to known URLs instead of reflecting the raw query parameter.

findings.title: NoSQL operator injection in login username lookup
findings.attack_path: validateLogin passes userName straight into usersCol.findOne({userName}). bodyParser.json() lets a client send an object instead of a string, so a JSON body like {"userName":{"$gt":""},"password":...} (combined with the cleartext password comparison in TM-003) can match an unintended user document and subvert the authentication query.
findings.remediation: Coerce userName and password to strings and reject non-string types before querying. Use a schema validator and enable a MongoDB query sanitizer (e.g. reject keys beginning with $).

findings.title: Broken authentication: weak password policy, user enumeration, and no brute-force protection
findings.attack_path: validateSignup enforces only PASS_RE=/^.{1,20}$/ (any 1-20 chars), and handleLoginRequest returns distinct 'Invalid username' vs 'Invalid password' messages with no rate limiting or lockout. An attacker enumerates valid usernames, then runs unthrottled credential-stuffing/brute-force against trivially weak passwords to take over accounts.
findings.remediation: Require strong passwords (length and complexity per the commented PASS_RE fix), return an identical generic error for both failure modes, and add rate limiting plus account lockout/backoff and optional MFA.

findings.title: Verbose error responses disclose stack traces
findings.attack_path: errorHandler renders error-template with the full error object and logs err.stack. Triggering an unhandled error (e.g. malformed contribution input reaching next(err)) returns internal file paths, library versions, and stack details that aid an attacker in mapping the codebase and chaining other flaws.
findings.remediation: Return a generic error page to clients in production, log full details server-side only, and never serialize the raw error/stack into the response.

findings.title: Vulnerable and outdated dependencies and EOL runtime
findings.attack_path: package.json pins known-vulnerable versions (marked 0.3.5 with XSS/ReDoS advisories, mongodb ^2.1.18, swig 1.x) and the Dockerfile uses node:12-alpine, which is end-of-life and no longer patched. The memos Markdown path (TM-004) depends on marked's sanitizer, which is bypassable in 0.3.5; unpatched runtime CVEs widen the blast radius.
findings.remediation: Upgrade to maintained major versions of marked, mongodb, swig/consolidate; rebuild on a supported Node LTS base image; and add automated dependency/CVE scanning (npm audit, Dependabot) to CI.

findings.title: Log injection / log forging via unsanitized username
findings.attack_path: On a failed login, handleLoginRequest logs the raw userName ('attempt to login with invalid user: ' + userName). An attacker submits a username containing CRLF and forged log lines to inject fake entries, corrupt log integrity, and frustrate incident forensics, undermining repudiation controls.
findings.remediation: Encode/strip CR/LF from user input before logging (e.g. the ESAPI encodeForHTML or userName.replace(/(\r\n|\r|\n)/g,'_') fix noted in session.js) and prefer structured logging that escapes field values.

findings.title: Container hardening disabled and missing resource limits
findings.attack_path: In the Dockerfile the recursive chown/chmod hardening line is commented out, and docker-compose.yml sets no CPU/memory limits, read-only filesystem, or dropped capabilities. Combined with RCE (TM-001) or ReDoS (TM-013), a compromised process has broad filesystem write access and can exhaust host resources, easing escape and lateral movement.
findings.remediation: Run as a least-privileged non-root user with a read-only root filesystem and dropped capabilities, enable the commented chmod hardening, and set container resource limits in compose/orchestration.
